constellation.Cas: Look for a W or M made of five bright stars; its orientation varies with time and season.
constellation.Cyg: Follow the large cross of the Northern Cross: Deneb marks one end and Albireo the other.
constellation.Lyr: Spot Vega, very bright, then the small parallelogram of stars that accompanies it.
constellation.Ori: Look for the three almost aligned stars of the Belt, then the four stars that draw the hunter's body.
constellation.Sco: Look for Antares, a reddish star, then follow the long curve that evokes the Scorpion's tail.
constellation.UMa: First spot the seven stars of the Big Dipper: the edge opposite the handle helps find Polaris.
constellation.UMi: The Little Dipper forms a small saucepan; Polaris is at the end of its handle.
constellation.intro: Choose a figure: the main stars, its drawing then its remarkable landmarks will be presented step by step.
constellation.tip: Start by spotting the brightest stars of the figure; not all of their names are common.
constellation.walkTip: First spot the brightest star, then slowly follow the golden strokes from one star to the next. Compare the figure to the map, taking into account its orientation in the sky.

events.detailAnnularSolar: Never look at the Sun without a certified solar filter.
events.detailDeepSkyWindow: Around the New Moon, the absence of strong moonlight favors observing faint galaxies and nebulae, under a dark and clear sky.
events.detailFirstQuarter: The Moon is half illuminated and becomes more bothersome as the night goes on.
events.detailLeonids: The radiant lies in the constellation Leo; favor a dark sky.
events.detailMarsJupiter: Two planets to look for in the same region of the sky before dawn.
events.detailMinimalMoonlight: Moonlight is minimal: generally favorable period for deep sky if the weather is good.
events.detailMoonNearPleiades: Spot the Moon and the Pleiades cluster in the same region of the sky.
events.detailNorthernTaurids: Diffuse shower, active over a fairly long period.
events.detailOrionids: Best observed in the second part of the night; activity can extend over several nights around the maximum.
events.detailPenumbralLunar: Subtle darkening of the Moon; visibility depends on the horizon and local time.
events.detailPerseids: To observe after nightfall and until dawn, away from lights.
events.detailQuadrantids: Brief maximum: the hours around the peak matter especially.
events.detailSouthernTaurids: Few meteors on average, but possibility of bright fireballs.
events.detailTotalSolar: A total eclipse occurs over a limited geographic band; the visible phase depends on your location.
events.detailUrsids: A more modest winter shower, associated with the Little Dipper.
events.detailWaningCrescent: The Moon usually rises later: the first part of the night can be favorable for deep sky.
events.detailWaxingGibbous: Moonlight often hinders the observation of faint galaxies and nebulae.
events.disclaimer: Lunar phase dates are calculated by approximation. Events and favorable windows are indications: weather, light pollution and the local horizon remain decisive.

session.goalAstroAdvice: To start, photograph the Moon with a phone held firmly or a camera on a tripod. If the Moon is absent, try a star field with a short exposure, then gradually increase exposure time while watching for trails.
session.goalDiscoveryAdvice: Spot the Big Dipper, then extend the alignment of the two stars on the edge of the saucepan up to Polaris. It is a good first exercise to orient yourself in the sky.
session.goalGalaxiesAdvice: Try the Andromeda galaxy (M31, especially interesting under a dark autumn sky) or the Orion nebula (M42, winter target). Use binoculars first if you have them; a telescope requires a dark sky and low magnification.
session.goalMoonPlanetsAdvice: Start with the Moon if it is present: observe the boundary between lunar day and night, where reliefs stand out well. Then, check in Celestial Atlas which planets are above the horizon at the chosen time.
session.goalStarsAdvice: Compare the W shape of Cassiopeia with the Big Dipper, then look for Polaris between the two regions of the sky. Take the time to connect the brightest stars of each figure.
session.guideStep1Text: Choose a clear spot and check clouds, wind and Moon.
session.guideStep2Text: Let your eyes adjust to the dark, then identify an easy constellation.
session.guideStep3Text: Start with the naked eye or binoculars, then use a telescope if you have one.
session.guideStep4Text: Write down the time, the target and an impression; a short observation is already a success.
session.guideWarning: Tip: avoid white lights and never observe the Sun without a certified suitable solar filter.

mercury.fact: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. Despite its proximity, its nights are freezing: it has almost no atmosphere to retain heat. Its orbit lasts 88 Earth days.

venus.composition: Rocky planet with a very dense CO₂ atmosphere
venus.fact: Venus is covered by thick clouds that reflect sunlight very effectively. Its extreme greenhouse effect makes it the hottest planet, and it rotates in the opposite direction to most planets.

earth.composition: Rocky planet with oceans and a nitrogen–oxygen atmosphere
earth.fact: Earth is the only known planet that hosts life. Liquid water covers about 71% of its surface, and its atmosphere protects living things while regulating temperature.

mars.composition: Rocky planet; dust rich in iron oxides
mars.fact: Mars is home to Olympus Mons, the largest known volcano in the Solar System. Valleys and minerals point to a past in which liquid water played an important role.

jupiter.composition: Gas giant, mostly hydrogen and helium
jupiter.fact: Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System. Its Great Red Spot is a vast storm observed for centuries. Its four large Galilean moons can be spotted with ordinary binoculars.

saturn.composition: Gas giant, mostly hydrogen and helium
saturn.fact: Saturn’s rings are enormous but surprisingly thin. They consist of pieces of ice and rock, and the planet’s average density is lower than water’s.

uranus.composition: Ice giant with an atmosphere rich in hydrogen, helium and methane
uranus.fact: Uranus rotates almost on its side, causing extreme seasons. Methane in its atmosphere absorbs some red light and contributes to its blue-green colour.

neptune.composition: Ice giant with an atmosphere rich in hydrogen, helium and methane
neptune.fact: Neptune is so far from the Sun that it takes nearly 165 Earth years to complete an orbit. Extremely fast winds sweep through its atmosphere despite the weak input of solar energy.

solarSystem.defaultPlanetFact: The planet closest to the Sun.

ui.discoveryCluster: is a star cluster. An open cluster draws a group of stars in the Milky Way; a globular cluster forms a very dense ball of ancient stars. Binoculars often reveal numerous members.
ui.discoveryComet: is a comet: a small icy body that can release gas and dust as it approaches the Sun. Its position is calculated by a simplified orbital model; its actual brightness may differ strongly from predictions.
ui.discoveryDwarfPlanet: is a dwarf planet orbiting the Sun. Its position on the map is calculated with a simplified orbital model; a professional ephemeris remains preferable for high-precision pointing.
ui.discoveryGalaxy: is a galaxy: a vast ensemble of stars, gas and dust bound by gravity. To the naked eye or binoculars, it most often appears as a faint diffuse glow, very sensitive to sky quality.
ui.discoveryGeneric: is a celestial object whose appearance depends on its nature, sky quality and the instrument used.
ui.discoveryMinorPlanet: is an asteroid orbiting the Sun. Its position on the map is calculated with simplified orbital propagation; a professional ephemeris remains preferable for high-precision pointing.
ui.discoveryNebula: is a nebula, a cloud of gas and/or dust. Depending on its nature, it can illuminate forming stars or consist of matter ejected by a dying star; its details depend heavily on the sky and the instrument.
ui.discoveryPlanet: is a planet in the Solar System. Its distance, apparent size and perceptible details change according to its position in its orbit; a very bright point to the naked eye does not necessarily reveal its surface.
ui.discoveryStar1: is a star in the Milky Way
ui.discoveryStar2: . Its color and apparent brightness help compare it to neighboring stars; its twinkling also depends on the atmosphere.

ui.factEarth: Mean diameter: 12,742 km. Liquid water on the surface and nitrogen- and oxygen-rich atmosphere.
ui.factJupiter: Mean diameter: about 139,820 km. Gas giant with many moons and cloud bands.
ui.factMars: Mean diameter: 6,779 km. Thin atmosphere and surface marked by volcanoes and canyons.
ui.factMercury: Mean diameter: 4,879 km. Extremely thin atmosphere; heavily cratered surface.
ui.factMoon: Diameter: about 3,475 km. Its surface keeps many impact craters.
ui.factNeptune: Mean diameter: about 49,244 km. Ice giant with very fast winds.
ui.factSaturn: Mean diameter: about 116,460 km. Gas giant famous for its ring system.
ui.factSun: Diameter: about 1.39 million km. G2 V type star, photospheric temperature near 5,780 K.
ui.factUranus: Mean diameter: about 50,724 km. Ice giant with a strongly tilted rotation axis.
ui.factVenus: Mean diameter: 12,104 km. Very dense atmosphere, mostly CO₂.

ui.glossaryTerms: Apparent magnitude: apparent brightness (the smaller the number, the brighter the object). RA and declination: coordinates locating the object on the celestial sphere. Azimuth: direction on the horizon, counted from north toward east. Altitude: height above the horizon (0° at the horizon, 90° at the zenith). Seeing (turbulence): atmospheric agitation that blurs details. Transparency: sky clarity; haze, dust and humidity attenuate faint objects.

explanation.01: Never observe the Sun directly without a certified solar filter suitable for the instrument and mounted at its front.
explanation.02: The target is currently below the horizon. It can be searched for once it rises.
explanation.03: The atmosphere absorbs and blurs more light near the horizon. The target may be hard to distinguish; waiting until it rises often helps.
explanation.04: The Moon is usually easy to find without an instrument. Its phase changes the lighting on its surface; binoculars or a telescope reveal more detail.
explanation.05: It mainly appears as a bright point; seeing planetary details requires an instrument. Clouds, transparency and low altitude can make observing harder.
explanation.06: This planet may be visible, but that depends on its brightness and sky conditions. An instrument may help reveal its details.
explanation.07: No apparent magnitude is available; the visibility of this dwarf planet cannot be estimated from the catalogue.
explanation.08: Even the brightest dwarf planets are difficult to detect with the naked eye. Light pollution and sky transparency are decisive.
explanation.09: Dwarf planets look like faint starlike points; an instrument is required.
explanation.10: A dwarf planet may remain difficult to identify with binoculars; carefully compare the field and its calculated position.
explanation.11: This dwarf planet is generally too faint for ordinary binoculars. A telescope and a detailed chart are useful.
explanation.12: A telescope may be sufficient depending on its aperture and conditions; the calculated position is simplified and should be compared with a recent ephemeris.
explanation.13: This dwarf planet is very faint. Use suitable equipment and check its position against an up-to-date ephemeris.
explanation.14: Dwarf planets are faint points of light. The displayed magnitudes and positions are estimates; they are not a substitute for a precision ephemeris.
explanation.15: No apparent magnitude is available; the visibility of this minor planet cannot be estimated from the catalogue.
explanation.16: Even among the brightest asteroids, finding one with the naked eye is demanding. Light pollution and sky transparency are decisive.
explanation.17: Minor planets generally look like faint starlike points. Most require binoculars or a telescope.
explanation.18: The magnitude suggests that trying with binoculars may be possible under a dark sky, but finding the object remains difficult and requires a detailed chart.
explanation.19: This minor planet is probably too faint for ordinary binoculars. A telescope and a comparison star field will be useful.
explanation.20: Telescopic pointing is preferable. The magnitude is estimated from a simplified orbital model; compare the position with a recent ephemeris.
explanation.21: This minor planet may require suitable equipment, a transparent sky and precise pointing. Check its position against an up-to-date ephemeris.
explanation.22: Minor planets are faint points of light. The displayed magnitudes and positions are estimates; they are not a substitute for a precision ephemeris.
explanation.23: No apparent magnitude is available; it is not possible to make a reliable estimate of how easy the object is to find from the catalogue alone.
explanation.24: The star is bright. Light pollution and sky transparency can nevertheless reduce contrast near the horizon.
explanation.25: Stars of this brightness are easier to see when the sky is dark and transparent and your eyes are dark-adapted.
explanation.26: This star may be too faint in a city or through haze. Binoculars or a much darker sky may be needed.
explanation.27: The star should be within reach of ordinary binoculars if the sky is clear; steady the binoculars to find it more comfortably.
explanation.28: Detection depends on binocular aperture, stability and how dark the sky is.
explanation.29: This star may be beyond the reach of ordinary binoculars. More powerful equipment and a dark sky will help.
explanation.30: The star should be within reach of many amateur telescopes; focus, aperture and atmospheric conditions all matter.
explanation.31: Detection depends on aperture, magnification, transparency and observing experience.
explanation.32: This star is faint. Suitable equipment, accurate tracking and a transparent sky may be necessary.
explanation.33: Generally visible to the naked eye if it is high enough and the horizon is clear.
explanation.34: It may be visible to the naked eye under a dark sky; in a city or through cloud haze, binoculars may help.
explanation.35: It may be difficult to see with the naked eye. Binoculars or a telescope, along with a dark sky, may be needed.
explanation.36: The magnitude is unavailable; apparent size and the concentration of stars also affect the cluster’s visibility.
explanation.37: The cluster may look like a small patch or pattern of stars. Its total magnitude does not guarantee that individual stars will be separated; a dark sky helps.
explanation.38: The cluster’s total brightness is low for the naked eye. Binoculars are generally more suitable, although visibility also depends on the cluster’s apparent size and the sky.
explanation.39: Binoculars work well for many open clusters. Globular clusters may remain diffuse patches; a dark sky improves contrast.
explanation.40: A dark sky is important; a telescope may be needed, especially to distinguish individual stars.
explanation.41: A telescope can reveal more stars, but the result depends on aperture, magnification and cluster type.
explanation.42: Detecting and resolving the stars requires suitable equipment and a transparent sky.
explanation.43: Total magnitude alone does not indicate how many stars will be visible. Aperture and observing conditions are decisive.
explanation.44: It may appear as a patch or pattern of stars; binoculars often reveal more of its structure.
explanation.45: A cluster may require binoculars or a telescope. Integrated brightness does not guarantee that its stars can be separated.
explanation.46: The cluster is faint overall; the result depends on its concentration, aperture and sky transparency.
explanation.47: Galaxies and nebulae are diffuse: only a few exceptions can be perceived under a very dark sky. Total magnitude alone cannot predict their contrast against the sky background.
explanation.48: Some targets appear as a faint patch under a dark sky. Surface brightness, transparency and light pollution matter as much as total magnitude.
explanation.49: A telescope may reveal a patch or structure depending on the object, but details are not guaranteed. Total magnitude does not adequately describe surface brightness; filters and sky conditions can change the result.
explanation.50: For diffuse objects, integrated magnitude alone cannot predict what the eye will see. Surface brightness, light pollution, transparency, dark adaptation and equipment are all decisive.
explanation.51: This estimate is indicative only: altitude, transparency, light pollution and the equipment actually used all affect the result.
explanation.52: The Andromeda Galaxy may appear as a faint smudge under a very dark, transparent sky; in light-polluted areas it may be invisible.
explanation.53: The Orion Nebula may be perceived as a diffuse glow, but not with the colourful details seen in photographs. Transparency and light pollution matter greatly.

universe.descCosmicWeb: At very large scale, galaxies group into clusters and organize into filaments separated by immense voids. The Universe is about 13.8 billion years old. As space expanded while light travelled, the diameter of the observable Universe is today estimated at about 93 billion light-years.
universe.descLocalGroup: The Milky Way is part of the Local Group, a set of dozens of galaxies dominated by the Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy. Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away.
universe.descMilkyWay: The Sun lies in the disc of the Milky Way, in the local arm called the Orion Arm, about 26,000 light-years from the galactic centre. The galaxy contains hundreds of billions of stars.
universe.descNearby: The Sun belongs to a neighbourhood of stars. Proxima Centauri, the closest known star after the Sun, lies about 4.24 light-years away. Distances between stars far exceed the dimensions of planetary systems.
universe.descSolar: The Solar System spans about 100 astronomical units (AU) in this educational frame. One AU is the average Earth–Sun distance, about 149.6 million kilometres. The eight planets orbit the Sun, but distances are too large to be faithfully represented at this scale.
universe.milkyWayPointer: ✦ Our position in the Milky Way
universe.noteCosmicWeb: Didactic diagram, not a real or to-scale map: filaments and clusters are deliberately spaced to make the structure readable.
universe.noteLocalGroup: Sizes and distances between galaxies are compressed to fit the view.
universe.noteMilkyWay: Schematic top view: spiral arms are complex structures, not fixed rails.
universe.noteNearby: Stars are drawn to be visible; their sizes and spacings are schematic.
universe.noteSolar: Chosen frame: about 100 AU, i.e. 14.96 billion kilometres. The edge of the Solar System depends on what is considered (planetary orbits, distant regions or the Sun’s influence); the drawing remains schematic.
universe.scaleLocalGroup: Local Group · scale of several galaxies
universe.titleCosmicWeb: The cosmic web and the observable Universe

visibleNow.disclaimer: Visibility depends on the location and date selected. Presence above the horizon does not guarantee that the object is visible to the naked eye.
visibleNow.helpText: The selection favours objects above 10° and suggests a few targets according to their type and catalogue magnitude. The 'Spotting' label is an educational estimate based on height, type, magnitude and chosen equipment, not a guarantee of visibility. Light pollution, transparency, surface brightness and experience change the result; diffuse objects can be difficult even with a favourable integrated magnitude. When calculable, culmination indicates when the target passes highest in the sky.

walk.andromedaIntro: M31 is a neighbouring galaxy to ours. Under a dark sky, it appears to the naked eye as a small blurry patch, not as a sharp star.
walk.andromedaStep1: Spot the Great Square of Pegasus, which serves as a starting point in the autumn sky.
walk.andromedaStep2: From Alpheratz, the star at one corner of the Great Square of Pegasus, follow the chain of stars of Andromeda toward Mirach, then toward Mu Andromedae.
walk.andromedaStep3: Near Mu Andromedae, look a little to the side of the alignment: under a dark sky, M31 resembles a small elongated and diffuse glow. If you don't see it, choose a darker location and let your eyes adapt.
walk.andromedaTip: M31 is much easier under a dark sky, without a bright Moon or light pollution. It is especially well placed in the evening in autumn and early winter.
walk.dipperToArcturusIntro: The Big Dipper's handle allows you to find two bright stars: Arcturus then Spica. It is a classic landmark for learning the spring sky.
walk.dipperToArcturusStep1: Spot the two stars on the edge of the Big Dipper, Merak and Dubhe.
walk.dipperToArcturusStep2: Follow the curve of the handle to Alkaid, then extend the arc to find Arcturus, bright and orange.
walk.dipperToArcturusStep3: Continue in the same direction to reach Spica, in Virgo. The classic mnemonic is 'arc to Arcturus, spike to Spica'.
walk.dipperToArcturusTip: The path is especially handy in spring. The line is an approximate guide, not an exact trajectory.
walk.dipperToArcturusTitle: From the Big Dipper to Arcturus
walk.orionIntro: Orion is one of the easiest silhouettes to learn, especially on winter evenings.
walk.orionStep1: Spot three stars fairly close together and almost aligned: this is Orion's belt.
walk.orionStep2: Above and to the left of the belt, look for Betelgeuse, often recognizable by its orange tint.
walk.orionStep3: On the other side, Rigel shines with a white-blue glow. The belt, Betelgeuse and Rigel allow you to find the hunter's silhouette.
walk.orionTip: Orion is especially visible in the evening during late autumn and winter.
walk.pleiadesIntro: The Pleiades are a tight small group of stars that resembles a tiny ladle or a small sparkling cloud.
walk.pleiadesStep1: Start by spotting the constellation Taurus or the bright Aldebaran, with its orange appearance.
walk.pleiadesStep2: Look a little further for a small compact packet of several bluish stars: these are the Pleiades, also called the Seven Sisters.
walk.pleiadesStep3: Observe them first with the naked eye. With binoculars, many more stars appear in the same field.
walk.pleiadesTip: The Pleiades are particularly easy to observe on autumn and winter evenings. They remain an extended object: avoid looking for them with high magnification.
walk.polarisIntro: The Big Dipper serves as a signpost. You don’t need to know the stars by name to begin.
walk.polarisStep1: Find the Big Dipper: it looks like a large saucepan with a handle.
walk.polarisStep2: Find the two stars on the edge opposite the handle: Merak and Dubhe. Extend the line from Merak toward Dubhe, then continue beyond Dubhe about five times their separation.
walk.polarisStep3: You arrive near Polaris. It marks approximately celestial north and is at the end of the handle of the Little Dipper, more discreet.
walk.polarisTip: The Big Dipper and Polaris are circumpolar from metropolitan France: they generally remain above the horizon.
walk.springTriIntro: Three bright stars, in three different constellations, form a wide triangle easy to memorize.
walk.springTriStep1: Spot Arcturus, a very bright orange star, by extending the arc of the Big Dipper's handle.
walk.springTriStep2: Find Regulus in Leo to close the triangle: Arcturus, Spica and Regulus are the three vertices.
walk.springTriTip: The spring triangle is especially notable in spring and early summer in the northern hemisphere.
walk.summerIntro: Three very bright stars draw a large triangle in the sky of late spring and summer evenings.
walk.summerStep1: Look for Vega, very bright and almost white-blue. It is in the small constellation of Lyra.
walk.summerStep2: Spot Deneb further to the northeast, in Cygnus, whose stars draw a large cross.
walk.summerStep3: Find Altair to the south of the triangle, in Aquila. Vega, Deneb and Altair together form the Summer Triangle.
walk.summerTip: The triangle is especially practical in summer and early autumn; its height depends on the time and season.
walk.winterHexIntro: Six very bright stars draw a large outline in the winter sky. Betelgeuse lies inside this figure.
walk.winterHexStep1: Start with Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, then spot Rigel in Orion.
walk.winterHexStep2: Continue along the outline toward Aldebaran, with its orange look, then Capella, very bright higher in the sky.
walk.winterHexStep3: Continue toward Pollux, then Procyon, before returning to Sirius: you have traced the great winter hexagon.
walk.winterHexTip: This figure is mostly visible on winter evenings. The stars must be above the horizon and a clear sky helps a lot.
walk.springTriStepMiddle: From Arcturus, look lower in the sky for Spica, in Virgo.

descriptions.M1: Remnant of the supernova observed in 1054; a pulsar lies at its center.
descriptions.M13: A very dense globular cluster containing hundreds of thousands of stars.
descriptions.M27: A planetary nebula formed from the outer layers shed by a dying star.
descriptions.M31: A large spiral galaxy near the Milky Way, accompanied by several satellite galaxies.
descriptions.M42: A star-forming region illuminated by young, hot stars.
descriptions.M44: A nearby open cluster, also known as the Beehive Cluster.
descriptions.M45: A young open cluster known as the Pleiades.
descriptions.M51: A spiral galaxy interacting with a smaller companion galaxy.
descriptions.M57: A ring-shaped planetary nebula: a shell of gas expelled by an aging star.
descriptions.M81: A large spiral galaxy in the M81 Group.
descriptions.M82: A galaxy with intense star formation, commonly called the Cigar Galaxy.
descriptions.M104: A spiral galaxy seen almost edge-on, recognizable by its dust lane.
descriptions.NGC253: A bright spiral galaxy in Sculptor, seen at a moderate angle.
descriptions.NGC457: An open cluster whose brightest stars resemble an owl.
descriptions.NGC869/884: Two neighboring open clusters known together as the Double Cluster in Perseus.
descriptions.NGC1499: An emission nebula known as the California Nebula.
descriptions.NGC3372: A large star-forming region in the constellation Carina.
descriptions.NGC4755: A colorful open cluster nicknamed the Jewel Box.
descriptions.NGC5139: Omega Centauri, one of the Milky Way’s most massive globular clusters.
descriptions.NGC4565: An almost edge-on spiral galaxy nicknamed the Needle Galaxy.
descriptions.NGC7000: An emission nebula whose outline resembles North America.
descriptions.NGC7293: A nearby planetary nebula nicknamed the Helix Nebula.
descriptions.NGC6888: An emission nebula shaped by the winds of a massive star.
descriptions.SOLEIL: The star at the center of the Solar System; its light takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.
descriptions.LUNE: Earth’s natural satellite; its phase and position change throughout the month.

discoveryDescriptions.M1: The Crab Nebula is the debris cloud left by an exploding star. At its center, a pulsar spins rapidly: the compact remnant of that star.
discoveryDescriptions.M3: A nearly spherical globular cluster where hundreds of thousands of very old stars are held closely together by gravity.
discoveryDescriptions.M13: The Great Hercules Cluster is a globe of ancient stars. Through a telescope, its outer regions resolve into countless tiny points of light.
discoveryDescriptions.M27: The Dumbbell Nebula is a shell of gas blown off by an aging star; its shape resembles a dumbbell or an apple core.
discoveryDescriptions.M31: The Andromeda Galaxy is a vast spiral galaxy with a bright core and star-filled arms. Its light has been travelling to us for about 2.5 million years.
discoveryDescriptions.M33: The Triangulum Galaxy is a rather diffuse spiral, rich in regions where new stars are born; it is best viewed under a dark sky.
discoveryDescriptions.M42: The Orion Nebula is a stellar nursery: young, hot stars illuminate the gas around them.
discoveryDescriptions.M44: The Beehive Cluster contains many relatively young stars. To the naked eye it can look like a small hazy patch; binoculars separate its stars.
discoveryDescriptions.M45: The Pleiades are a young group of blue-white stars born together. Binoculars reveal their arrangement much better than the naked eye.
discoveryDescriptions.M51: The Whirlpool Galaxy is a spiral whose arms are highlighted by gravitational interaction with its smaller companion.
discoveryDescriptions.M57: The Ring Nebula is a shell of gas expelled by a star nearing the end of its life. Its small disk requires enough magnification to distinguish it from a star.
discoveryDescriptions.M81: Bode’s Galaxy is a fairly bright large spiral. Its companion, the Cigar Galaxy (M82), can be seen in the same region of the sky.
discoveryDescriptions.M82: The Cigar Galaxy is elongated and undergoing intense star formation, probably stimulated by interactions with its neighbor M81.
discoveryDescriptions.M104: The Sombrero Galaxy is seen almost edge-on: its bright central bulge and broad dark dust lane give it the appearance of a hat.
discoveryDescriptions.SIRIUS: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is a relatively nearby white star. Its strong twinkling near the horizon is mainly caused by the atmosphere.
discoveryDescriptions.VEGA: Vega is a very bright white star in Lyra. It is part of the Summer Triangle and helps you find this small constellation.
discoveryDescriptions.ARCTURUS: Arcturus, an orange giant in Boötes, is one of the brightest stars in the sky. Its warm color contrasts with the whiter nearby stars.
discoveryDescriptions.BETELGEUSE: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant at Orion’s shoulder. Its diameter is enormous and its brightness varies slightly over time.
discoveryDescriptions.RIGEL: Rigel, a brilliant blue star at Orion’s foot, is much hotter and intrinsically brighter than the Sun.
discoveryDescriptions.POLARIS: Polaris lies close to the direction of the north celestial pole: stars appear to circle around it during the night.
discoveryDescriptions.JUPITER: Jupiter is a gas giant with bands of clouds; its four largest moons can be seen as tiny points in a line with binoculars or a telescope.
discoveryDescriptions.SATURNE: Saturn is a gas giant whose rings, made mostly of ice and rocky fragments, are especially recognizable through a telescope.
discoveryDescriptions.MARS: Mars is a rocky planet whose iron-oxide-rich dust gives it an orange-red color. When it is close to Earth, a telescope may reveal its polar cap and dark markings.
discoveryDescriptions.VENUS: Venus is covered in highly reflective clouds. Through a telescope it shows phases like the Moon, but its clouds hide the surface.
discoveryDescriptions.ALDEBARAN: Aldebaran is an orange giant that appears to mark the Bull’s eye. It looks close to the Hyades cluster in the sky, but is actually much nearer to us.
discoveryDescriptions.ALTAIR: Altair is one of the three stars of the Summer Triangle. It spins rapidly, making it slightly flattened at the poles.
discoveryDescriptions.DENEB: Deneb marks the Swan’s tail. It is an extremely luminous supergiant that remains visible to the naked eye despite its great distance.
discoveryDescriptions.CAPELLA: Capella is the bright star of Auriga. It is actually a multiple-star system, including two yellow giants very close to each other.
discoveryDescriptions.POLLUX: Pollux is an orange giant in Gemini. A planet has been discovered orbiting it, making it one of the bright stars known to host an exoplanet.
discoveryDescriptions.SPICA: Spica is the brightest star in Virgo. It consists of two very hot stars orbiting so closely that they are strongly distorted.
discoveryDescriptions.M8: The Lagoon Nebula contains dark dust lanes that carve through its glowing cloud. It hosts several regions where stars are forming.
discoveryDescriptions.NGC7000: The North America Nebula is a vast region of ionized hydrogen. Its distinctive outline is best seen in wide-field photographs.
discoveryDescriptions.NGC1499: The California Nebula is very elongated. Its low surface brightness makes it difficult to see without a suitable filter and a dark sky.

observingAdvice.star: Find it using nearby stars. Stars remain point-like in most telescopes; aim for precise focus and observe when the atmosphere is steady.
observingAdvice.planet: Observe it when it is high above the horizon to reduce atmospheric distortion. Medium to high magnification may reveal details, depending on the planet and atmospheric steadiness.
observingAdvice.sun: WARNING: Never look at the Sun without a certified solar filter mounted at the front of the instrument. Sunglasses and eyepiece filters are not safe.
observingAdvice.moon: Lunar relief is especially high-contrast near the terminator, the boundary between lunar day and night. Binoculars already reveal many details.
observingAdvice.galaxy: Choose a dark site away from artificial lights. Start with low magnification and use averted vision; galaxies often look much fainter to the eye than in photographs.
observingAdvice.nebula: A dark sky makes a big difference. Try low magnification; a suitable filter can improve the view of some nebulae, but not all.
observingAdvice.cluster: Open clusters are excellent targets for binoculars. A telescope and steady sky help resolve more stars in globular clusters.
observingAdvice.deep-sky: Choose a dark sky and start at low magnification. The view through an eyepiece may be much less contrasty than astronomical photographs.

discoveryChallenges.star: Compare its color with a nearby star: does it look bluer, whiter or more orange?
discoveryChallenges.planet: Find a bright nearby star and compare how they twinkle: a planet often appears steadier.
discoveryChallenges.sun: Observe only by using a suitable projection method or a certified solar filter designed for your instrument.
discoveryChallenges.moon: Find the boundary between the lit and dark areas: shadows there bring the lunar relief into view.
discoveryChallenges.galaxy: Let your eyes adapt to the dark and look slightly to one side to make the faint glow easier to detect.
discoveryChallenges.nebula: First observe without looking for color: try to make out the overall shape and brightest areas.
discoveryChallenges.cluster: Count a few stars, then widen your view: how many more can you see around them?
discoveryChallenges.deep-sky: Start by finding the indicated area, then give your eyes time to adapt to the darkness.

discoveryFacts.M1: The Crab Nebula preserves the trace of a stellar explosion observed in 1054.
discoveryFacts.M13: This globular cluster contains hundreds of thousands of stars packed tightly together by gravity.
discoveryFacts.M27: This nebula is a shell of gas expelled by a star near the end of its life.
discoveryFacts.M31: The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away: its light began travelling before our species appeared.
discoveryFacts.M42: New stars are forming from gas and dust inside the Orion Nebula.
discoveryFacts.M45: The Pleiades are a young group of stars born together in the same cloud of gas.
discoveryFacts.M57: The visible ring is gas expelled by a star. Our Sun may undergo a similar stage in the very distant future.
discoveryFacts.M51: The two galaxies interact gravitationally; their encounter helps shape the spiral arms.
discoveryFacts.M104: The Sombrero Galaxy’s dark lane is a broad band of dust seen edge-on.
discoveryFacts.SOLEIL: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel the distance to Earth.
discoveryFacts.LUNE: The Moon almost always shows us the same face because its rotation is synchronized with its orbit around Earth.
discoveryFacts.JUPITER: Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System; its cloud bands are visible through a telescope.
discoveryFacts.SATURNE: Saturn’s rings are made of countless pieces of ice and rock.
discoveryFacts.MARS: Mars gets its red color mainly from iron oxides in its dust.
discoveryFacts.VENUS: Venus is often very bright because its clouds reflect much of the sunlight.

catalogue.description: Educational selection of numbered asteroids and the five dwarf planets (Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake). Orbital elements come from published tables; positions are calculated with a simplified Keplerian model, without planetary perturbations, and are not precision JPL Horizons ephemerides. The comets also use simplified Keplerian propagation from reference orbital elements; their brightness is particularly uncertain and their positions do not replace an up-to-date ephemeris.

encke.discoveryNote: A periodic comet known for its frequent returns; its 2027 apparition is worth watching.

halley.discoveryNote: A famous periodic comet observed since antiquity; its next perihelion passage is expected in 2061.

churyumovGerasimenko.discoveryNote: A comet studied up close by ESA’s Rosetta mission.

haleBopp.discoveryNote: The great comet of 1997, notable for its long orbital period.

neowise.discoveryNote: A bright comet of summer 2020, now very distant and no longer visually observable.

hartleyIras.discoveryNote: A comet to look for with a telescope through the end of 2026, according to available forecasts.

gaiaReviewReasons.propagationResidual: Gaia DR3 association retained, but it should be reviewed: the residual between the Gaia position at epoch 2016.0 and the propagated Hipparcos position exceeds the combined formal uncertainties calculated without covariances. The Gaia source has a two-parameter astrometric solution (position only); do not use Gaia proper motion for propagation. Photocentre/component effects may still be present in multiple systems.
gaiaReviewReasons.positionOnlyCrossCheck: Cross-checked with SIMBAD; Gaia DR3 astrometric_params_solved=3 (position only), with no parallax or proper motion. Here, gaia_match_arcsec is the offset from the search centre in catalogue coordinates, not a residual after epoch propagation; do not use it as a definitive astrometric residual.
gaiaReviewReasons.propusPositionOnly: Gaia DR3 association provisionally retained and cross-checked with SIMBAD (η Geminorum / Propus). The historical value 2.262″ previously recorded as gaia_match_arcsec could not be reproduced in the Gaia DR3 Hipparcos cross-match tables and matches phot_g_mean_mag rounded to 2.262; it is therefore retained only as a reported value, not as a verified separation. A search around the currently recorded Hipparcos coordinates finds the source at 1.68281″, but this separation compares positions from different epochs and is not an epoch-corrected astrometric residual. Gaia DR3 provides a position-only solution here, with no parallax or proper motion; do not propagate this source.
